summary: In international civil space policy, Croatia has officially signed the NASA-led Artemis Accords, while NASA selected a far-infrared telescope as the first mission in a new class and marked 200,000 orbits for the Hubble Space Telescope. In defense developments, the United Kingdom launched its first military space squadron dedicated to protecting satellites and degrading enemy assets, and reports indicate SpaceX was granted unique access to classified U.S. Department of Defense space tracking data. Meanwhile, the U.S. Air Force and Space Force are accelerating research into orbital cargo delivery, with the Space Force seeking maneuverable spacecraft for on-demand launch capabilities while working to bolster its supply chain. Commercial space activity expanded as Vast announced a new Lunar Programs Division, Outpost debuted an in-space manufacturing service, Astrolab partnered with Interstellar Mapping to search for lunar water, and HEO raised $25 million in Series B funding for geostationary coverage. On the scientific front, sample analysis from the asteroid Bennu points to an unexpected origin involving Jupiter, astronomers detected radio signals from an exoplanet for the first time, and research indicates silicon solar cells could cut satellite power costs by up to 90 percent. Looking ahead, industry observers should watch for a pending Federal Communications Commission vote on waiving environmental reviews for space operations.
